title: How a reversible transition amplifies apparent entropy production
shortTitle: Waiting-time entropy estimates can overshoot without bound
oneLine: A counterexample to the uncorrected waiting-time inequality of Harunari, Fiore and Barato, and the sharp correction for blocks of waits.
abstract: Experiments on small driven systems, such as molecular motors and colloids in moving traps, usually see only a few transitions and the waiting times between them, so dissipation is estimated from waiting-time statistics. For periodically driven systems, Harunari, Fiore and Barato proposed comparing waiting-time histograms recorded with the driving protocol and with the protocol reversed, without recording the phase of the drive. They proved that this estimate minus a correction X is a lower bound on entropy production and left open whether the uncorrected estimate is one as well. This candidate shows that it is not, and that its excess is unbounded. In a smooth three-state model with zero period-averaged current on every edge, equal event rates in both experiments and fixed entropy production 4π/5, the estimate grows linearly with the rate of one reversible transition: an exact rational certificate proves more than 31 times the entropy production at one rate, and a certified lag-bin bound more than 145 times. The failure persists when every microscopic jump is recorded, and under a small constant cycle affinity, under which the model numerically pumps a net current. For every finite driven network, the estimate from blocks of m consecutive waits exceeds the phase-resolved bound by at most X/m, where X needs only the phase histogram of each kind of visible event, and the coefficient cannot be lowered; if events sample the phase reversal-symmetrically, the uncorrected estimate is safe. Harunari, Fiore and Barato's corrected inequality remains valid. Limits: a model calculation; the overshoot per event is small and needs a reporter several hundred times faster than the drive; the scaling table and sharpness are proved for the example only. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 1 (proof and exact certificate): in a three-state model with zero period-averaged current on every edge, equal event rates in both experiments and entropy production 4π/5, the uncorrected phase-blind estimate satisfies S₁ ≥ R[17/600 − 2C/R]₊², so it exceeds 31 times the entropy production at R = 100,000 and is unbounded relative to it.

Proposition 2 (exact certificates): certified lag-bin bounds give S₁ > 366.44 at R = 100,000, more than 145 times the entropy production; the smallest certified violation is at R = 750, about 375 reporter events per period.

Section 4 and Corollary 3 (proof): the violation persists when all six directed jumps are recorded, and under a small constant cycle affinity for any R ≥ 5400; numerically the model then pumps a net current, and at R = 1000 the binned ratio stays between 1.10 and 1.53 for affinities up to 1.

Theorem 5 (proof, every finite driven network): the block estimate of m consecutive waits satisfies 0 ≤ S_m ≤ σ_L + X/m ≤ σ + X/m; the case m = 1 is Harunari, Fiore and Barato's corrected inequality, which remains valid.
Corollary 6 (proof): S₁ − σ ≤ X, and if visible events sample the drive phase reversal-symmetrically then X = 0 and the uncorrected estimate is a lower bound for every block length.

Theorem 7 and Section 6 (proof, for the example): the coefficient of X/m cannot be lowered; the block estimate is determined in every scaling regime, with a phase-recovery transition at blocks of order R^(2/3) waits.

narration:
Tiny machines such as molecular motors and beads in moving laser traps turn some of the energy they receive into heat. The rate of that heat production, the entropy production, tells us how hard the system is working. Experiments usually see only a few of its jumps and the waiting times between them, so physicists estimate dissipation from those waiting times.

For systems driven by a repeating rhythm, three physicists proposed a practical recipe. Run the experiment once with the rhythm and once with the rhythm reversed, compare the two histograms of waiting times, and never record where in the cycle each jump happened. They proved that this estimate, minus a correction, can never exceed the true dissipation, and they asked whether the estimate on its own is also safe.

This release shows that it is not. The example is a system with three states, in which every current averages to zero and the true dissipation is fixed. One transition is very fast and runs at the same rate in both directions, so it produces no heat at all. But its speed rises and falls with the drive, so it quietly reports where the system is in the cycle. Reversing the drive changes which speeds a typical wait samples, and the estimate counts that difference as dissipation. Exact arithmetic proves that the estimate can exceed the true value more than thirty-one times over, and a sharper certified bound gives more than a hundred and forty-five times, with no upper limit as the transition speeds up.

The release also proves a general repair. Using blocks of consecutive waits, the overshoot is never more than the correction divided by the block length, and that correction cannot be made smaller. The original corrected inequality remains valid.

The limits matter. This is a model calculation, the effect per jump is small, and it needs a transition hundreds of times faster than the drive. The practical lesson is simple: do not report the uncorrected estimate as a bound unless the visible jumps sample the cycle evenly.

decisionObject.description: Decide whether the phase-blind forward-versus-reversed waiting-time estimate of Harunari, Fiore and Barato can be reported as a lower bound on entropy production, and what correction makes block estimates safe.
decisionObject.scope: Finite continuous-time Markov jump processes with continuous periodic rates bounded away from zero; a three-state example; population distributions, not finite samples.
